Compositional lasso: penalized log-contrast regression

Source: R/coda_lasso.r
coda_lasso.Rd

Predicts an outcome (a measurement, or one of two classes) from a feature table and picks out the features that matter, in a way that respects compositionality: the log-contrast model (Aitchison & Bacon-Shone 1984; Lin et al. 2014), fitted with an elastic-net penalty and the penalty chosen by cross-validation. coda_lasso() constrains the features' coefficients to sum to zero, as zeroSum does (Altenbuchinger et al. 2017); coda_lasso_pairwise() puts the penalty on all pairwise log ratios, as coda4microbiome's coda_glmnet() does (Calle et al. 2023).

Usage

coda_lasso(
  counts,
  y,
  data = NULL,
  given = NULL,
  family = NULL,
  margin = 1L,
  pseudocount = NULL,
  l1_ratio = 1,
  lambda = NULL,
  n_lambdas = 100L,
  lambda_min_ratio = NULL,
  standardize = FALSE,
  n_folds = 10L,
  folds = NULL,
  select = c("min", "1se"),
  tol = 1e-08,
  max_iters = 100L,
  seed = 0L,
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

coda_lasso_pairwise(
  counts,
  y,
  data = NULL,
  given = NULL,
  family = NULL,
  margin = 1L,
  pseudocount = NULL,
  l1_ratio = 0.9,
  lambda = NULL,
  n_lambdas = 100L,
  lambda_min_ratio = NULL,
  standardize = TRUE,
  n_folds = 10L,
  folds = NULL,
  select = c("1se", "min"),
  tol = 1e-07,
  max_iters = 100000L,
  seed = 0L,
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

Arguments

counts

A numeric matrix of feature values (samples \(\times\) features), or any of the table types listed under "Input Types". Typically counts; any positive scale (counts, proportions, the output of replace_zeros()) gives the same fit.

y

What to predict: a vector with one value per sample, or the name of a column of data. Numeric y is a measurement (family = 'gaussian'); a factor, logical or character y with two values is a class ('binomial'; the second level, or TRUE, is the "event" whose log odds are modelled). Samples whose y is NA are left out, with a warning.

data

A data frame of sample metadata, with one row per sample (matched to counts by row names when both have them), when y, given or folds name its columns. Default: NULL

given

Covariates to adjust for (age, sex, BMI): a one-sided formula over the columns of data (such as ~ age + sex), the names of columns of data, or a data frame with one row per sample. coda_lasso() fits them alongside the features, unpenalized and outside the zero-sum constraint (zeroSum's penalty.factor = 0 and zeroSum.weights = 0); coda_lasso_pairwise() first regresses y on them alone and passes that fit as an offset (coda4microbiome's covar). Samples with NA in given are left out, with a warning; covariates that are linear combinations of others are dropped, with a warning. Default: NULL

family

'gaussian' (least squares) or 'binomial' (logistic regression), or NULL to choose from y (see y). Default: NULL

margin

The margin containing samples. 1 if samples are rows, 2 if samples are columns. Ignored when counts is a special object class (e.g. phyloseq). Default: 1

pseudocount

Value added to counts to handle zeros when norm = 'clr' or 'log'. Ignored for other normalization methods. See Pseudocount section.

l1_ratio

The elastic-net mixing parameter, between 0 (ridge) and 1 (lasso): the penalty is \(\lambda[(1 - r)/2 \|\beta\|_2^2 + r \|\beta\|_1]\). glmnet and zeroSum call it alpha. Default: 1 for coda_lasso() (zeroSum's), 0.9 for coda_lasso_pairwise() (coda4microbiome's).

lambda

The penalties to fit, or NULL for a path of n_lambdas values from the smallest that makes every coefficient zero down to lambda_min_ratio times it, evenly spaced on the log scale. Default: NULL

n_lambdas

The length of the default path. Default: 100

lambda_min_ratio

The smallest penalty of the default path, as a fraction of the largest; NULL for 0.01 when there are fewer samples than coefficients, else 1e-4 (zeroSum's and glmnet's rule). Default: NULL

standardize

Penalize each coefficient in proportion to the standard deviation of its column (log abundance, or log ratio), as if the columns were scaled to unit variance; the constraint and the reported coefficients stay on the original scale. Default: FALSE for coda_lasso() (zeroSum's), TRUE for coda_lasso_pairwise() (coda4microbiome's, through glmnet's default).

n_folds

The number of cross-validation folds, which choose \(\lambda\); 0 or 1 for none (then lambda must be a single value). Default: 10

folds

A fold for each sample instead (any labels; each label is a fold, as glmnet's and zeroSum's foldid), matched to the samples like y. Overrides n_folds and seed. Default: NULL

select

Which \(\lambda\) the result reports: 'min', the one with the best cross-validated error, or '1se', a larger (sparser) one within a standard error of it (see Details). Default: 'min' for coda_lasso() (zeroSum's), '1se' for coda_lasso_pairwise() (coda4microbiome's).

tol

The convergence tolerance: zeroSum's precision (the change in the cost function between sweeps) for coda_lasso(); glmnet's thresh (the largest change of any coefficient's contribution, relative to the null deviance) for coda_lasso_pairwise(). Default: 1e-8 and 1e-7.

max_iters

The most iterations: zeroSum's outer (active-set) steps for each \(\lambda\) in coda_lasso(); glmnet's maxit, the most passes over the coefficients in all, for coda_lasso_pairwise(). Default: 100 and 1e5.

seed

An integer seed for the folds. Default: 0

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), is the CPU cores this R process may use, within any limits set on it. Results are the same for any cpus.

Value

A data frame of class ecodive_coda_lasso (or ecodive_coda_lasso_pairwise), one row per feature in table order: feature, coefficient (\(\beta_j\) at the chosen \(\lambda\)) and selected (coefficient != 0). Its attributes:

method

'coda_lasso' or 'coda_lasso_pairwise'.

intercept, lambda, select, family, l1_ratio, pseudocount

The fit's intercept, the chosen \(\lambda\) and the rule that chose it, and the settings that qualify the coefficients.

covariates

With given: the covariates' coefficients (coda_lasso()), or those of the offset model (coda_lasso_pairwise(), with its intercept).

folds

Each sample's fold.

path

A data frame: lambda, cv_error, cv_se and n_selected, one row per \(\lambda\); cv_measure names the error ('mse', 'deviance' or 'auc').

coef_path

The features' coefficients along the path (features \(\times\) \(\lambda\)).

fitted

A data frame: sample, link (the linear predictor, the "signature score") and, for binomial y, probability; cv_link holds each sample's cross-validated linear predictor.

performance

Gaussian: r_squared (the squared correlation of the fitted and observed values), cv_mse and cv_mse_se. Binomial: auc (apparent), cv_auc and cv_auc_se (the folds' AUCs averaged as glmnet does, at the chosen \(\lambda\)).

y

The outcome as fitted (a factor for binomial y).

pairs

coda_lasso_pairwise() only: the non-zero \(\theta_{jk}\), a data frame of numerator, denominator and coefficient.

Details

The log-contrast model

For samples \(i\) and features \(j\), with \(g\) the identity (gaussian) or the logit (binomial), $$g(E[y_i]) = \beta_0 + \sum_j \beta_j \log x_{ij}, \quad \sum_j \beta_j = 0.$$ Because the coefficients sum to zero, multiplying a sample by any constant changes nothing: the fit is the same on counts, proportions or rarefied counts, and \(\sum_j \beta_j \log x_{ij} = \sum_j \beta_j \mathrm{clr}(x_i)_j\). The features with positive coefficients form the numerator, and those with negative ones the denominator, of a single weighted log ratio (the "signature"; Calle et al. 2023).

coda_lasso() minimizes $$-\frac{1}{n}\ell(\beta_0, \beta) + \lambda \sum_j \left[\frac{1 - r}{2} v_j^2 \beta_j^2 + r v_j |\beta_j|\right]$$ (\(\ell\) the log-likelihood, \(r\) = l1_ratio, \(v_j\) the column's standard deviation with standardize, else 1) subject to the constraint, by zeroSum's coordinate descent over pairs of coefficients (raising one while lowering another keeps the sum at zero). For gaussian y the ridge term is divided by the standard deviation of y, as zeroSum and glmnet do.

coda_lasso_pairwise() fits the same model through the log ratios of every pair of features, \(\log(x_j / x_k)\), \(j < k\), as coda4microbiome does: \(\beta_j = \sum_k \theta_{jk} - \sum_k \theta_{kj}\) sums to zero by construction, and the penalty falls on the \(\theta\). It never forms the \(n \times p(p-1)/2\) table of log ratios. With a pure lasso (l1_ratio = 1), no standardization and no covariates, its fit at \(2\lambda\) is coda_lasso()'s at \(\lambda\), since the cheapest \(\theta\) giving a \(\beta\) has \(\|\theta\|_1 = \|\beta\|_1 / 2\). With the defaults (standardized, l1_ratio = 0.9) they differ.

Choosing lambda

Each fold's samples are predicted from a fit to the others along the whole path. coda_lasso() follows zeroSum: the error is the mean squared error (gaussian) or the binomial deviance per sample, averaged over folds, with standard error \(\mathrm{sd}/\sqrt{K}\) over the \(K\) folds; '1se' is the \(\lambda\) (no smaller than the best) whose error is closest to the best error plus its standard error. coda_lasso_pairwise() follows cv.glmnet() as coda4microbiome calls it: the mean squared error (gaussian) or the AUC (binomial; the binomial deviance, with a warning, when there are fewer than 10 samples per fold, as glmnet does), averaged over folds weighted by their size; '1se' is the largest \(\lambda\) whose error is within a standard error of the best. The default path stops early, as glmnet's does, once the fit explains 99.9% of the deviance or stops improving.

Folds are drawn at random with seed (for binomial y, within each class, so that each fold has both). Penalized fits come with no p-values: a feature's selection is not a test of it.

Zeros and covariates

Zeros have no logarithm: replace them first (see replace_zeros()), or a pseudocount is added (see "Pseudocount" below).

Differences from zeroSum and coda4microbiome

  • zeroSum: the largest penalty of the default path includes every pair of features (zeroSum's lambdaMax skips the first feature), and with given it is computed from the residuals of y on the covariates; the path is always fitted to its end (zeroSum's cvStop = 0.1 stops it once the CV error rises); folds are drawn with ecodive's random numbers (and stratified by class); max_iters caps zeroSum's fixed 100 outer steps. Coefficients agree with zeroSum's to its convergence tolerance; both reach the same cost to about 1e-10.

  • coda4microbiome: zeros get ecodive's shared pseudocount rule (coda4microbiome adds 1, or half the smallest value below 1, to every value); coefficient is \(\beta\) as fitted, not rescaled to \(\sum|\beta| = 2\); the apparent \(R^2\) and AUC are computed whether or not features are selected (coda4microbiome reports 0 and 0.5 when none are); the reported CV AUC is the AUC even when the deviance chose \(\lambda\). glmnet's solution is matched to its tolerance, not its iterations.

Same names in other packages

None known.

Machine learning

Log-ratio transforms (clr, rclr, alr, ilr, PhILR) serve interpretation and compositional geometry; don't expect them to improve prediction. With random forests predicting 65 metadata variables in four datasets, Yerke et al. (2024) found that alr, clr and ilr (PhILR) "performed generally slightly worse or only as well as compositionally naïve transformations", and relative abundances did best, by a small margin. Compare with norm = 'percent' (see normalize()) before choosing a log-ratio predictor table.

Input Types

The counts parameter is designed to accept a simple numeric matrix, but seamlessly supports objects from the following biological data packages:

  • phyloseq

  • rbiom

  • SummarizedExperiment

  • TreeSummarizedExperiment

For large datasets, standard matrix operations may be slow. See vignette('performance') for details on using optimized formats (e.g. sparse matrices) and parallel processing.

Pseudocount

The pseudocount parameter is only relevant when norm = 'clr' or norm = 'log'.

Zeros are undefined in the centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation and in the log of proportions. If norm is 'clr' or 'log', pseudocount is NULL (the default), and zeros are detected, the function uses half the minimum non-zero value (min(x[x>0]) / 2) and issues a warning.

To suppress the warning, provide an explicit value (e.g., 1), or replace the zeros first with replace_zeros(), whose result needs no pseudocount.

Why this matters: The choice of pseudocount is not neutral; it acts as a weighting factor that can significantly distort downstream results, especially for sparse datasets. See Gloor et al. (2017) and Kaul et al. (2017) for open-access discussions on the mathematical implications, or Costea et al. (2014) for the impact on community clustering.

See aitchison for references.

References

Aitchison, J., & Bacon-Shone, J. (1984). Log contrast models for experiments with mixtures. Biometrika, 71, 323-330. doi:10.1093/biomet/71.2.323

Lin, W., Shi, P., Feng, R., & Li, H. (2014). Variable selection in regression with compositional covariates. Biometrika, 101, 785-797. doi:10.1093/biomet/asu031

Altenbuchinger, M., Rehberg, T., Zacharias, H. U., et al. (2017). Reference point insensitive molecular data analysis. Bioinformatics, 33, 219-226. doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btw598

Calle, M. L., Pujolassos, M., & Susin, A. (2023). coda4microbiome: compositional data analysis for microbiome cross-sectional and longitudinal studies. BMC Bioinformatics, 24, 82. doi:10.1186/s12859-023-05205-3

Susin, A., Wang, Y., Lê Cao, K.-A., & Calle, M. L. (2020). Variable selection in microbiome compositional data analysis. NAR Genomics and Bioinformatics, 2, lqaa029. doi:10.1093/nargab/lqaa029

Friedman, J., Hastie, T., & Tibshirani, R. (2010). Regularization paths for generalized linear models via coordinate descent. Journal of Statistical Software, 33(1), 1-22. doi:10.18637/jss.v033.i01

Tibshirani, R., Bien, J., Friedman, J., et al. (2012). Strong rules for discarding predictors in lasso-type problems. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 74, 245-266. doi:10.1111/j.1467-9868.2011.01004.x

See also

predict.ecodive_coda_lasso(), plot.ecodive_coda_lasso(), log_ratio(), random_forest()

Examples

    # Which features predict a measurement? 30 samples, 8 features.
    set.seed(1)
    counts <- matrix(rpois(240, 50), 30, 8, dimnames = list(NULL, LETTERS[1:8]))
    y      <- log(counts[, 'A'] / counts[, 'B']) + rnorm(30, sd = 0.1)
    fit    <- coda_lasso(counts, y, n_folds = 5, cpus = 1)
    fit
#> Compositional Lasso, gaussian y: a data.frame 8 × 3
#> lambda = 1.25e-06 (min), l1_ratio = 1: 8 of 8 features selected
#> Apparent R^2 0.828; cross-validated MSE 0.0109 +/- 0.00255
#> Numerator (coefficient > 0): A (1.29), G (0.137), E (0.131), D (0.0703)
#> Denominator (coefficient < 0): B (-1.2), F (-0.348), C (-0.0675), H
#>   (-0.0156)
#> # Attributes: method, intercept, lambda, select, family, l1_ratio,
#> #   pseudocount, folds, path, cv_measure, coef_path, fitted, cv_link,
#> #   performance, y

    # The same with all pairwise log ratios.
    coda_lasso_pairwise(counts, y, n_folds = 5, cpus = 1)
#> Compositional Lasso (pairwise log ratios), gaussian y: a data.frame 8 × 3
#> lambda = 0.0417 (1se), l1_ratio = 0.9: 3 of 8 features selected
#> Apparent R^2 0.787; cross-validated MSE 0.0132 +/- 0.00323
#> Numerator (coefficient > 0): A (0.874)
#> Denominator (coefficient < 0): B (-0.821), F (-0.0533)
#> # Attributes: method, intercept, lambda, select, family, l1_ratio,
#> #   pseudocount, folds, path, cv_measure, coef_path, fitted, cv_link,
#> #   performance, y, pairs
